'''Albert Erives''' (born March 4, 1972) is a developmental geneticist who studies transcriptional [[Enhancer (genetics)|enhancers]] underlying [[Developmental biology|animal development]] and diseases of development ([[cancer]]s). Erives also proposed the pacRNA model for the dual origin of the [[genetic code]] and [[homochirality|universal homochirality]].<ref name="pacRNA">{{cite journal | author = Erives A | title = A Model of Proto-Anti-Codon RNA Enzymes Requiring L-Amino Acid Homochirality | journal = Journal of Molecular Evolution | volume = 73 | issue = 1–2 | pages= 10–22 | year = 2011 | pmid = 21779963 | doi = 10.1007/s00239-011-9453-4 | pmc=3223571| bibcode = 2011JMolE..73...10E }}</ref> He is known for work at the intersection of [[genetics]], [[evolution]], [[developmental biology]], and [[gene regulation]].<ref name=mg2>{{cite journal | author = Crocker, J. |author2=Tamori, Y. |author3=Erives, A. |name-list-style=amp | title = Evolution acts on enhancer organization to fine-tune gradient threshold readouts | journal = PLOS Biology | volume = 6|issue=11 | year = 2008 | pmid = 18986212 | doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.0060263 | pmc=2577699 | article-number=e263 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=Myc>{{cite journal | author = Brown, S. |author2=Cole, M. |author3=Erives, A.J. |name-list-style=amp | title = Evolution of the holozoan ribosome biogenesis regulon | journal = BMC Genomics | volume = 9| page =442| year = 2008 | pmid = 18816399 | doi = 10.1186/1471-2164-9-442 | pmc=2570694 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="EAC">{{cite journal | author = Erives, A. | title = Erives has shown how genes of the [[nucleocytoplasmic large DNA viruses]] inform on intermediate steps in the evolution of the linear, [[chromatin]]ized eukaryotic chromosome and its mechanisms of [[Regulation of gene expression|gene regulation]].<ref name="NRG-euk">{{cite journal | author = Talbert, P. | author2= Meers, M.P.| author3= Henikoff, S.| title = Old cogs, new tricks: the evolution of gene expression in a chromatin context. | journal = Nature Reviews Genetics | year = 2019 | volume= 20| issue= 5| pages= 283–297| pmid = 30886348 | doi = 10.1038/s41576-019-0105-7 | s2cid= 81987181}}</ref><ref name="MV-core">{{cite journal | author = Erives, A.| title = Phylogenetic analysis of the core histone doublet and DNA topo II genes of Marseilleviridae: evidence of proto-eukaryotic provenance. | journal = Epigenetics & Chromatin | year = 2017 |volume=10 | issue=55| page = 55 | pmid = 29179736 | doi = 10.1186/s13072-017-0162-0 | pmc=5704553 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Regulatory grammars of enhancers ==
Erives' major work is on "regulatory grammars" for transcriptional [[Enhancer (genetics)|enhancers]]  underlying animal [[developmental biology|development]] and [[cancer|cancer diseases]]. Exploiting assemblies for animal genomes, Erives discovered complex gene regulatory codes underlie non-homologous subsets of mechanistically equivalent enhancers.<ref name=Myc/><ref name=EAC/><ref name=spikey/> These codes are composed of a combinatorial "lexicon" of [[transcription factor]] (TF) binding sites, functional inflections of those binding sites (so-called "specialized sites" constrained for binding affinity and competition by multiple TFs), and complex site ordering (orientation and positional spacing of those sites). The relationship of these complex regulatory codes within a nucleosomal "regulatory reading frame" is a key goal.<ref name=Stroebele/> His lab's work also elucidated how a mutational mechanism (microsatellite repeat slippage) plays a significant evolutionary role in functionally adjusting complex binding site arrangements that recruit poly-glutamine rich factors.<ref name=mg2/><ref name=mg3/><ref name="mg4">{{cite journal |title=Microsatellite repeat instability fuels evolution of embryonic enhancers in Hawaiian ''Drosophila'' |year=2015 |last1=Brittain |first1=A |last2=Stroebele |first2=E| last3=Erives |first3=A |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=9 |issue=6 |article-number=e101177 |pmid=24978198 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0101177 |pmc=4076327|doi-access=free }}</ref> Correspondingly, Erives lab has pioneered the identification of novel poly-glutamine complex recruiting enhancers that integrate developmental signals,<ref name="Stroebele">{{cite journal |title=Integration of Orthogonal Signaling by the Notch and Dpp Pathways in Drosophila |year=2016 |last1=Stroebele |first1=E |last2=Erives |first2=A |journal=Genetics |volume=203 |issue=1 |pages=219–240 |pmid=26975664 |doi=10.1534/genetics.116.186791 |pmc=4858776}}</ref> while also identifying polyQ allelic series for key developmental factors targeting those enhancers.<ref name="pmid26362765">{{cite journal | vauthors = Rice C, Beekman D, Liu L, Erives A | title = The Nature, Extent, and Consequences of Genetic Variation in the opa Repeats of ''Notch'' in ''Drosophila'' |journal=G3: Genes, Genomes, Genetics |volume=5 |issue=15 | pages=2405–2419|date=2015 |pmid=26362765 | doi=10.1534/g3.115.021659 | pmc=4632060}}</ref>

A significant implication of this work is that [[gene regulatory networks]] largely evolve by [[indels]] in both ''cis'' and ''trans'' (in enhancer DNAs and polyQ-encoding genes, respectively). As indels are largely produced by unstable [[microsatellite|microsatellite repeats]], which are fast-evolving and difficult to genotype accurately, a large compartment of functional genetic variation is not treated by [[genome-wide association study|genome-wide association studies]], which focus on [[single nucleotide polymorphisms]] and at most a subset of non-repeat associated indels.

== Molecular determinants of morphogenic responses ==

Erives and colleagues determined how different [[morphogen|morphogen gradient responses]] are encoded in DNA sequence.<ref name=mg2/><ref name=mg3/> They did so by using diverse ''[[Drosophila]]'' species that have different sized [[egg (biology)|egg]]s to study how a set of structured [[enhancer (genetics)|enhancer]]s<ref name=EAC/><ref name=spikey>{{cite journal |author1=Erives, A. |author2=Levine, M. | title =Coordinate enhancers share common organizational features in the ''Drosophila'' genome | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume = 101 | pages = 3851–3856 | year = 2004 | pmid = 15026577 | issue=11 | doi=10.1073/pnas.0400611101 | pmc=374333|bibcode=2004PNAS..101.3851E |doi-access=free }}</ref> would have co-evolved or co-adapted to changes in the concentration gradients. Morphogen gradient systems are a core fundamental subject of [[developmental biology]]. Models of how morphogen gradient responses were encoded had previously been proposed but not tested across a set of unrelated [[enhancer (genetics)|enhancers]] constructed from a shared regulatory grammar and located throughout a [[genome]].

Three major unexpected findings resulted from this work. The first finding is that gradient responses in general do not evolve by changes in [[transcription factor]] (TF) binding site quality or quantity (site density) as expected, but rather by changes in the precise spacing between binding sites for morphogenic TFs and their partner TFs.<ref name=mg2/> The second finding is that homotypic site clustering at such enhancers was largely the result of a complex evolutionary history of selection for different threshold responses in the [[evolution|evolving]] [[insect]] [[egg (biology)|egg]].<ref name=mg3/> A third-related finding is that frequent selection for different responses also enriches for [[Microsatellite|microsatellite repeat tracts]], which are inherently unstable and most responsible for the production of novel [[indel]] alleles.<ref name=mg3/><ref name=mg4/>

Erives' work also showed the existence of inherent spatial-temporal conflict in morphogenic responses and how this is handled in nature via complementary morphogenic gradients.<ref name=spacetime>{{cite journal |author1=Crocker, J. |author2=Erives, A. | title =A Schnurri/Mad/Medea complex attenuates the dorsal-twist gradient readout at ''vnd''. | journal = Developmental Biology | volume = 378 | pages = 64–72 | year = 2013 | pmid = 23499655 | issue=1 | doi=10.1016/j.ydbio.2013.03.002| doi-access =free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://now.uiowa.edu/2013/05/developmental-genetics-space-and-time|title = The developmental genetics of space and time|date = 15 May 2013}}</ref>

== Molecular determinants of the genetic code ==
Using insights gleaned from [[archaea]]l genomes, Erives elaborated and described a [[stereochemistry|stereochemical]] model of "proto-anti-codon RNAs" (pacRNAs).<ref name=pacRNA/> The pacRNA model ascribes a predetermined combined origin for the universal [[genetic code]] (''i.e.'', the codon table), the biogenic amino acids, and their exclusive [[homochirality]] in life. The model implies that early [[RNA world]] was  an aminoacylated RNA world and that [[proteinogenic amino acid]]s arose because of compatible interactions with nucleotide-based polymers. The pacRNA model explicitly lists possible interactions between various anti-codon di-nucleotide and tri-nucleotide sequences and different amino acids. When the nucleotides are D-ribose based, L-amino acids are preferred.

In the pacRNA world, codons originate as ''cis''-elements for recruiting self-aminoacylated pacRNAs/proto-tRNAs. Thus, a curious aspect of this model is that the (anti-) codon table is determined in evolutionary history prior to the origin of [[ribosome]]-based [[translation (biology)|protein translation]]. The pacRNA model may explain why extant [[tRNA]]s are heavily [[RNA modification database|modified]] in all [[three-domain system|three domains of life]].

Erives first presented the pacRNA model at [[NASA]]s 2012 [[Astrobiology]] Science Conference<ref>2012 [[Astrobiology]] Science Conference. url: http://abscicon2012.arc.nasa.gov/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130214034622/http://abscicon2012.arc.nasa.gov/ |date=2013-02-14 }}</ref> and most recently at the 2013 Iowa City Darwin Day festival,<ref>2013 Iowa City Darwin Day. url: http://icdarwin.org {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190116035802/http://www.icdarwin.org/ |date=2019-01-16 }}</ref> which focused on the [[abiogenesis|origins of life]] on Earth.

Like Erives' enhancer studies, which focus on how protein complexes interact with enhancer DNAs, his pacRNA work focuses on how biogenic amino acids would have beneficially interacted with the nucleotide-based molecules of early life. Both areas of study demonstrate how complex patterns in linear molecules emerge from interactions in 3-dimensions.

== Developmental genetics in chordates ==
With his doctoral advisor [[Michael Levine (biologist)#Ciona|Michael Levine]], Erives authored several papers on [[ascidian]] [[developmental biology|developmental genetics]], with key insights into the evolution of the proto-vertebrate body plan.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Erives, A. |author2=Levine, M.| title = Cis-regulation of ascidian tail muscle genes. | journal = Proceedings of the First International Symposium on the Biology of Ascidians. Springer-Verlag, Tokyo 2001 | year = 2001}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Erives, A. |author2=Levine, M. | title = Characterization of a maternal T-box gene in Ciona intestinalis.| journal = Developmental Biology | volume = 225 | pages= 169–178 | year = 2000 | pmid = 10964472| doi = 10.1006/dbio.2000.9815 | issue=1| doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Erives, A. |author2=Corbo, J.C. |author3=Levine, M. | title = Lineage-specific regulation of the Ciona snail gene in the embryonic mesoderm and neuroectoderm. | journal = Developmental Biology | volume = 194 | pages= 213–225 | year = 1988 | pmid =9501022| doi =10.1006/dbio.1997.8810 | issue=2|s2cid=13229344 | doi-access = free }}</ref> This work used the ''[[Ciona]]'' system to generate copious amounts of embryos that were then electroporated with enhancer DNAs.

In collaboration with Nori Satoh's lab at the [[University of Kyoto]] in Japan, where Erives spent a winter doing research, they also identified the largest collection of [[notochord]] specific genes by using genetically altered ''Ciona'' over-expressing the [[Brachyury]] transcription factor.<ref>{{cite journal |author1= Takahashi, H. |author2=Hotta, K. |author3=Erives, A. |author4=Di Gregorio, A. |author5=Zeller, R.W. |author6=Levine, M. |author7=Satoh, N. | title = Brachyury downstream notochord differentiation in the ascidian embryo. | journal = Genes & Development | volume = 13 | issue = 12 | pages= 1519–1523 | year = 1999 | pmid =10385620| doi = 10.1101/gad.13.12.1519 | pmc=316807}}</ref> The [[notochord]] is a defining evolutionary innovation of the [[chordate]] body plan and this work was designed to advance understanding of the morphogenetic signals emanating from this important developmental and structural tissue.

== CodeGrok, Inc. ==
In 2001, Erives co-founded the [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]]-associated company CodeGrok (code "grok")<ref>https://www.bloomberg.com/research/stocks/private/snapshot.asp?privcapId=4925495</ref> with Paul Mineiro, currently a Principal Research Software Developer for [[Microsoft]].  It was started in [[Pasadena, California]] but later moved to [[Berkeley, California]] after its second round of financing. In its first three years, CodeGrok developed and used [[machine learning]] methods to identify, classify, and clone transcriptional enhancers from the human genome and construct pathway-specific cell-based reporters for drug screening and other applications.  The company took its name from the [[Robert Heinlein]] novel [[Stranger in a Strange Land]] and its concept of ''[[grok]]'', which is to understand something deeply and intuitively, in reference to the goal of "grokking" the regulatory code of the human genome. While the company is no longer in existence, it is often cited as a humorous example of what not to do in naming a start-up company as many people were unable to pronounce the name.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.brandingstrategyinsider.com/2010/10/technology-and-pharma-brand-naming.html#.WAU763qPzXs|title=Exploring Technology and Pharmaceutical Naming|date=30 October 2010}}</ref>
